newsitem.title: USA: Gaming amendments ouster a boost for Arkansas Amend. 4.
newsitem.headline: Gaming amendments ouster a boost for Arkansas Amend. 4.

text.p: The Arkansas Supreme Court's Monday decision to strike three of four proposed gambling amendments from the November 5 ballot helps the odds that the remaining constitutional amendment will pass, one of its supporters said Wednesday.
"I think it helps us. I think it helps the voters," said Craig Douglass, campaign coordinator for the surviving amendment, Amendment 4.

"Voters can now focus on the fact that amendment 4 is the only amendment on the ballot in November that will offer a state lottery, legalized charity bingo and authorized Hot Springs casinos if approved by local voters."
According to Arkansas Deputy Attorney General Tim Humphries, the Supreme Court jettisoned the three amendments, amendments 5, 7 and 8, because their summaries were either incomplete or misleading.
Supporters of those measures have until Friday to petition for a rehearing, he said.

Douglass said the precusor of the current Amendment 4 met a similar fate in 1994, when it was removed from the ballot. This time around, Amendment 4 is much simpler, he said. The new version is eight pages long, down from 22 in 1994, he said.

"We followed the Supreme Court decision two years ago, and followed exactly what they said amendments should be," Douglass said. Amendments should be "simple, and fair, and short and to the point," he said.
Douglass said Amendment 4 and stricken amendments contained similar provisions but varied in the scope of gaming each would allow.

All contained a lottery and charity bingo, along with some other form of gaming. Amendments 7 and 8 would have called for casinos as does Amendment 4. Under Amendment 4, however, the casinos would hinge on local voters approval. Amendment 5 had proposed video terminal games regulated by a Lottery Commission.

Under Amendment 4, it would be up to voters in Hot Springs National Park to decide whether to build three casinos there. But even if Hot Springs voters oppose the casinos, the state would still have a lottery and charity bingo, Douglass said.
